```{=html}
<!--
Notes on Video 1 (project setup + self-contained rendering):
- A .qmd mixes text and R code chunks. Rendering executes the code and
  produces a combined output document (HTML by default; PDF needs LaTeX
  installed; Word also possible but HTML is what this course wants).
- Keep data files in a data/ subfolder and images in an images/ subfolder
  inside the project, alongside the .qmd, so file paths stay simple.
- By default, rendering can dump supporting files into a separate folder
  next to the HTML -- fine normally, but not what you want for submitting
  a single file.
- Fix: embed-resources: true under format > html (already in the YAML
  above -- this is the current Quarto name for what used to be called
  "self-contained" in R Markdown). Bundles everything into one HTML file.
-->
```

# Iron Maiden

## Band Members

My favorite band members are:

-   Adrian Smith
-   Dave Murray

## Logo

![Iron Maiden's logo](images/IM-red_white_blackoutline-1-01.svg){#fig-logo fig-alt="A picture of Iron Maiden's logo"}

[Visit their website](https://www.ironmaiden.com)

@fig-logo shows the band's logo.

```{=html}
<!--
Note: the {#fig-logo ...} tag after the image is a cross-reference label.
Once labeled this way, don't manually type "Figure 1" in the caption --
Quarto auto-numbers it based on order of appearance, and @fig-logo in the
text becomes a clickable hyperlink straight to the image. Label must start
with "fig-" for it to be recognized as a figure.
-->
```

### Spotify Data

I got this data using the `spotifyr` package.

{r}
library(readr)
library(spotifyr)
eddie_tib \<- here::here("data/eddiefy.csv") \|\> read_csv()
eddie_tib \|\>
dplyr:: sample_n(10) \|\>
knitr:: kable(caption = "Spotify data for the band Iron Maiden", digits = 2)

{r}
#\| label: preview-data
head(tracks)

@fig-scatter shows the relationship between valence and energy scores for Iron Maiden studio tracks.

{r}
#\| label: fig-scatter
#\| fig-cap: "Scatter plot of the energy and valence scores for Iron Maiden tracks, 1980 to 2021"
ggplot(tracks, aes(x = valence, y = energy)) +
geom_point()

@tbl-spotify shows data from the Spotify API for Iron Maiden's studio albums.

{r}
#\| label: tbl-spotify
#\| tbl-cap: "Data from the Spotify API for Iron Maiden studio albums, 1980 to 2021"
knitr::kable(head(tracks))

# References

```         
```

A few notes worth keeping in your actual codebook comments, since this is the densest lecture yet:

Citations (`Insert` → `Citation`) need a bibliography file to write to — the dialog will prompt you to create one the first time (YAML, BibTeX, or CSL-JSON; YAML is fine) and that's the `references.bib` referenced in the YAML above. You don't need Zotero for this — the same dialog lets you search "From DOI" or search PubMed/Crossref directly, which is the path to use if you don't have a reference manager set up. Toggling "Insert in-text citation" on gives you `Author (Year)` style; off gives you a bracketed citation. Once you've inserted at least one citation and added the `# References` heading at the bottom, Quarto auto-populates that section on render — you never type the reference list by hand.

The `@fig-` / `@tbl-` cross-reference system is the standout feature from Part 5: any label starting with `fig-` or `tbl-` gets auto-numbered in order of appearance and turned into a clickable link wherever you reference it with `@label-name`, so if you later reorder sections, the numbering updates itself on the next render — no manual renumbering ever.

For the `#| label:` and `#| fig-cap:` lines inside code chunks — those are chunk options written Quarto-style (`#|` prefix) rather than the R-Markdown-style `{r label, fig.cap="..."}` in the header. Both exist; Quarto docs favor the `#|` style, which is what the video uses in Part 5.
